notes.meaning: David runs to the Lord for safety from enemies who are hunting him down. A man named Cush has spread false and damaging charges against him to the king. David calls the Lord "my God," resting in God's covenant promise to care for His own. When others attack us with lies, our first step should always be running to God in prayer.

David pictures his fiercest enemy as a ravenous lion ready to tear him to pieces. Without God's intervention, David knows he is completely helpless and has no human defender to save his life. The cruelty of the wicked is ruthless, but God is able to rescue His sheep from the jaws of beasts.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine understood this lion as the devil, who constantly prowls around seeking to devour believers through temptation and slander.

notes.meaning: David firmly denies the crimes his accusers laid against him. He never betrayed a friend or attacked an enemy without cause; in fact, he had spared King Saul's life when he had the chance to take it. He calls down extreme disaster on himself if these charges are true, willing to be crushed in the dust if he is guilty. A clear conscience before God brings tremendous boldness when people falsely accuse us.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that David was following the patience of Christ, and that verse 5 describes the natural spiritual ruin of those who repay good with evil rather than being a literal curse on himself.

notes.meaning: David calls on God to take His seat as judge and stop the cruel rage of his pursuers. It may feel as though God is asleep while the wicked run wild, but David asks Him to take public action now. He asks only for the fair and righteous judgment that God has already promised to give.

David envisions all the nations of the earth gathered around the Lord's great courtroom. He asks God to sit on His throne above them and declare what is right for everyone to see. When God defends the oppressed, all His people are drawn together to worship and praise Him.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine saw this gathering of the nations as a prophecy fulfilled when the Gentiles turned to faith in Jesus Christ after His resurrection and ascension.

notes.meaning: God is the supreme Judge over all people, and David asks Him to clear his name. David is not claiming to be sinless before God, but insists he is totally innocent of the treason and evil his enemies claim. Believers who have made peace with God can boldly ask Him to examine their actions and defend their integrity.

David prays for wickedness to come to a full stop everywhere, while the righteous are made secure. God searches through outward appearances to inspect the inner motives and secret thoughts of every person. Because the Lord knows our hearts so deeply, His decisions are always fair and completely right.

David declares that his defense comes from God alone. The Lord acts like a shield that protects those whose hearts are honest, pure, and sincere toward Him. We find lasting security when we trust God rather than human strength to guard our lives.

God is a completely just Judge who feels holy anger against persistent sin every single day. Even when ungodly people seem to prosper, God's disapproval remains upon their evil actions. God's delay in striking down sinners is not neglect, but a patient call giving them space to turn from their ways.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Ancient Greek and Latin versions, including the Catholic Vulgate, translate this verse to say that God is patient and 'not angry every day,' pointing to His longsuffering forbearance with sinners.

notes.meaning: If a person refuses to repent, God has His sword sharpened and His bow drawn to bring justice. Repent means turning away from sin and turning back to God. God gives clear warnings in advance so that no one has an excuse when judgment falls.

God keeps His deadly weapons ready for those who persist in doing harm. The fiery arrows picture swift and burning judgments sent against those who persecute God's people. Persecutors may think they have all the power on earth, but they can never put themselves beyond the reach of God's justice.

A wicked person works tirelessly to plan trouble, like a mother going through the pain of labor. He schemes and plots evil against others, but his effort only gives birth to lies and empty failure. Sin always promises success but ends in complete disappointment for the one who commits it.

The wicked dig a concealed pit to trap the innocent, but God causes them to tumble straight into their own ditch. The violent plots they aimed at other people bounce back directly onto their own heads. God governs the world so that evil designs ultimately destroy the very people who created them.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine noted that when God judges the wicked, He does not create new evils for them, but leaves them to suffer the natural destructive outcome of their own sins.

notes.meaning: David ends his prayer by singing joyful praise to the Lord Most High. He thanks God for His righteousness, confident that the Lord will keep His promises and defend the innocent. We can praise God with absolute joy even before our trials end, knowing His justice is sure to win.
